claims.claim: In transactions involving maker-controlled devices, buyers ordinarily pay money across a retail counter.
Devices sold under such arrangements ordinarily arrive as boxed products that buyers take into their homes.
Receipts for these transactions ordinarily characterize the device as the buyer’s property.
Makers can use remote commands to reduce a purchased device’s capacity.
Makers can use remote commands to reduce a purchased device’s compatibility.
Makers can use remote commands to reduce owners’ repair access.
Makers can use remote commands to remove a service for which a device buyer has paid.
Security patches can protect devices from security risks.
Network services may require controls against abusive use.
Subscriptions can expire pursuant to terms disclosed before purchase.
A maker-controlled kill switch gives the maker leverage over device repair.
A maker-controlled kill switch gives the maker leverage over device resale.
A maker-controlled kill switch gives the maker leverage over competition.
A maker-controlled kill switch affects when functioning products become waste.
Digital control over devices can be scaled at low marginal cost.
A locksmith must physically visit an individual car to alter or restore its lock access.
A vendor can change thousands of devices through a single policy action.
After checkout, buyers of maker-controlled devices bear sunk costs.
Makers can maintain a credible threat of changing purchased devices at low cost.
Refusing a device update can increase security risk.
Refusing a device update can impair compatibility.
Refusing a device update can cause loss of access.
Interoperability and repair rights make it practically possible for device owners to leave a maker-controlled product or service arrangement.
